title: Make incomplete work explicit and actionable
summary: Unresolved TODOs and FIXMEs should communicate remaining scope, risk, ownership, or a tracked follow-up.
guidance: Interview reviewers should be able to tell whether unfinished work is intentional, acceptable for the current scope, and safely tracked.

citation.title: Clutch clean-code reference: make incomplete work explicit

title: Use intentional observability at system boundaries
summary: Production behavior should rely on intentional logs or traces rather than stray debug prints.
guidance: Prefer structured logging where behavior crosses an API, job, or user workflow boundary, and remove local debugging output before review.

title: Make resource lifetime explicit
summary: Files, locks, transactions, and connections should have an obvious owner and deterministic cleanup path.
guidance: Use context managers or an equivalent lifecycle boundary so cleanup also occurs during exceptions and early returns.

title: Rubric: explain the maintenance cost of a change
summary: A strong junior-level review identifies future change points instead of labeling code as merely clean or messy.
guidance: Score the explanation higher when it names who will change the code, what must change together, and how drift would be detected.

citation.title: Clutch interview rubric: maintainable change scope

title: Question bank: future change scenario
summary: Ask which part of the implementation becomes hardest to change when a second caller or policy is added.
guidance: Look for a concrete change scenario, a named coupling point, and a proportionate refactoring rather than abstraction by default.

citation.title: Clutch question bank: future change scenario

title: Use names that expose purpose
summary: Names should distinguish intent, domain meaning, and units without forcing a reader to reconstruct them from implementation details.
guidance: Prefer specific domain names over vague placeholders, while keeping local names proportionate to their scope.

title: Document public behavior and contracts
summary: Public modules, classes, and functions should describe their contract where names and types do not communicate enough.
guidance: Document observable behavior, parameters, returns, and meaningful exceptions; avoid narrating syntax already visible in the code.

title: Write conditionals around the decision
summary: Conditional code should make the business decision visible without dense negation, unrelated side effects, or truthiness surprises.
guidance: Use direct comparisons where identity or sentinel behavior matters and extract a named predicate when the rule itself needs explanation.

title: Rubric: make the code explainable in one pass
summary: A strong interview explanation maps important names and branches to the behavior a reviewer should notice.
guidance: Score higher when the candidate distinguishes readability from personal style and identifies the actual comprehension cost.

title: Question bank: teammate handoff
summary: Ask what a teammate is most likely to misunderstand when they first modify this code.
guidance: Look for one concrete ambiguity, its consequence, and a small naming or control-flow improvement.

title: Preserve failure context with narrow error handling
summary: Catch only exceptions the code can handle and keep enough context to debug unexpected failures.
guidance: A bare except can hide programmer errors, interrupts, and runtime details that interviewers expect candidates to reason about.

title: Avoid shared mutable Python defaults
summary: Mutable default arguments are created once at function definition time and can leak state between calls.
guidance: Use None as the default for lists, dictionaries, and sets, then create a fresh object inside the function.

title: Keep time zones explicit at boundaries
summary: Naive and aware date-time values represent different contracts and should not be mixed implicitly.
guidance: Choose a boundary convention, preserve zone information where required, and test daylight-saving or offset behavior relevant to the product.

citation.title: Python datetime — Aware and Naive Objects

title: Rubric: name the failure model
summary: A strong answer explains what can fail, which failures are expected, and what observable behavior follows.
guidance: Score higher when the candidate covers invariants and failure behavior instead of describing only the happy path.

citation.title: Clutch interview rubric: correctness failure model

title: Question bank: find a counterexample
summary: Ask for the smallest input or state transition that would make the implementation return the wrong result.
guidance: Look for an explicit invariant, a plausible counterexample, and a test that distinguishes the fix from the original behavior.

title: Test behavior at meaningful boundaries
summary: Tests should cover expected behavior, important edge cases, and boundaries where code collaborates with other systems.
guidance: Prefer assertions about observable behavior over tests coupled to private implementation steps.

title: Keep tests deterministic and isolated
summary: A test should control the state, time, randomness, and external dependencies that affect its result.
guidance: Use setup and cleanup boundaries that prevent one test from changing the outcome of another, and make nondeterminism injectable.

title: Mock collaboration boundaries, not implementation details
summary: Mocks are most useful at a stable external boundary and become brittle when they mirror every private call.
guidance: Patch where a dependency is looked up, assert the behavior that matters, and avoid encoding an incidental call sequence unless it is the contract.

title: Rubric: connect each test to a risk
summary: A strong answer explains why each proposed test could catch a meaningful defect.
guidance: Score higher when the candidate covers happy, failure, and boundary cases and states what each assertion proves.

title: Question bank: verification matrix
summary: Ask for a compact matrix covering the happy path, one failure path, and one edge case.
guidance: Look for concrete inputs, observable outputs, and a reason each case protects against a distinct regression.

title: Keep units small enough to review and test
summary: Functions, classes, and snippets should be small enough that a reviewer can identify responsibilities and test boundaries.
guidance: Extract distinct decisions into named helpers when a unit grows large enough to obscure behavior, dependencies, or edge cases.

citation.title: Clutch clean-code reference: small reviewable units

title: Keep one source of truth for shared behavior
summary: Equivalent logic should have one implementation so fixes and policy changes cannot drift between copies.
guidance: Extract duplicated behavior into a clearly named helper while leaving callers responsible for their genuinely different context.

citation.title: Clutch clean-code reference: one source of shared behavior

title: Express dependencies through explicit boundaries
summary: Code is easier to test and replace when collaborators are passed through a narrow, typed protocol instead of discovered through global state.
guidance: Use the smallest interface the caller needs and keep construction separate from business behavior.

title: Rubric: justify a design boundary
summary: A strong answer connects a boundary to a concrete change, test, ownership, or failure concern.
guidance: Score higher when the candidate names a rejected alternative and avoids abstractions that have no current pressure.

citation.title: Clutch interview rubric: design boundary tradeoff

title: Question bank: introduce a second requirement
summary: Ask how the design changes when a second caller, storage system, or policy arrives.
guidance: Look for what remains stable, what becomes a boundary, and why the proposed abstraction is no larger than needed.

title: Keep query structure separate from untrusted values
summary: Database commands should use driver-supported parameter binding instead of interpolating values into SQL text.
guidance: Parameterization makes the trust boundary explicit and prevents input from changing the structure of a query.

citation.title: OWASP SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet

title: Validate untrusted input against the accepted contract
summary: Input validation should define acceptable syntax, length, range, and structure before data crosses a sensitive boundary.
guidance: Prefer allowlists and typed parsing for structured values; rejection and error responses should not expose sensitive internals.

title: Keep shell interpretation out of subprocess boundaries
summary: Passing untrusted text through a shell can turn data into commands or command arguments with unintended meaning.
guidance: Pass an argument sequence directly where possible, avoid shell execution, and validate any value that selects a program or path.

title: Rubric: identify the trust boundary
summary: A strong answer identifies which value is untrusted, what privileged interpreter receives it, and what validation or separation prevents control transfer.
guidance: Score higher when the candidate explains the attack path and defense rather than naming a vulnerability category alone.

citation.title: Clutch interview rubric: security trust boundary

title: Question bank: trace an attack path
summary: Ask how an attacker-controlled value moves from input to a privileged operation and where it should be constrained.
guidance: Look for source, transformation, sink, impact, and a defense that remains effective for adversarial input.

citation.title: Clutch question bank: trace an attack path

title: Make compatibility warnings actionable
summary: Deprecation and compatibility warnings should identify the affected behavior and the supported migration path.
guidance: Use a specific warning category, choose a useful caller-facing stack level, and remove obsolete paths on an explicit schedule.

title: Keep deploy-specific configuration outside code
summary: Configuration that varies between deployments should not require source changes or expose secrets in the repository.
guidance: Read configuration at the application boundary, validate it once, and pass typed settings to the code that needs them.

title: Communicate public compatibility through versions
summary: A public interface needs an explicit compatibility contract so callers can understand breaking and additive changes.
guidance: Describe the public API, classify changes consistently, and avoid silently changing behavior relied on by downstream callers.

title: Rubric: explain how the code is operated
summary: Maintainable code makes configuration, diagnosis, ownership, and safe change procedures visible to the next engineer.
guidance: Score higher when the candidate connects a code choice to debugging or deployment rather than discussing formatting alone.

title: Question bank: diagnose a production incident
summary: Ask which evidence would help a new engineer diagnose an unexpected production result in this path.
guidance: Look for structured signals, ownership boundaries, reproducible inputs, and a change that improves diagnosis without logging sensitive data.

title: Use type annotations to clarify contracts
summary: Type annotations should expose useful input, output, and callback contracts without restating what is already obvious.
guidance: Annotate public boundaries and complex shapes consistently; prefer a named protocol or model when a nested type obscures meaning.

title: Keep formatted values visible at the use site
summary: String formatting should make inserted expressions and formatting rules easy to associate with the resulting text.
guidance: Use a formatting form appropriate to the boundary, but never confuse readable presentation formatting with safe query or command parameterization.

title: Prefer explicit behavior over hidden cleverness
summary: A reader should be able to see the important decision and data transformation without relying on surprising implicit behavior.
guidance: Choose the simplest form that preserves the domain decision, and require a concrete benefit before using a denser idiom.

title: Rubric: identify the source of cognitive load
summary: A strong answer points to the exact name, branch, data shape, or side effect that forces unnecessary mental reconstruction.
guidance: Score higher when the proposed edit reduces a demonstrated comprehension cost instead of applying a style preference mechanically.

citation.title: Clutch interview rubric: readability cognitive load

title: Question bank: justify one rename
summary: Ask which single name would most improve a first-time reader's understanding and why.
guidance: Look for the hidden domain meaning, the misleading interpretation, and a replacement that remains proportionate to scope.

citation.title: Clutch question bank: justify one rename

title: Use decimal arithmetic when the domain requires exact decimals
summary: Binary floating-point cannot represent many decimal fractions exactly and can violate monetary or fixed-precision expectations.
guidance: Choose Decimal when exact base-ten arithmetic is part of the contract, construct values deliberately, and make rounding policy explicit.

citation.title: Python decimal — Decimal fixed-point and floating-point arithmetic

title: Choose shallow or deep copying deliberately
summary: Copying a container does not necessarily copy the nested mutable objects it references.
guidance: State whether identity sharing is part of the contract, and test mutation behavior when copying nested or recursive structures.

citation.title: Python copy — Shallow and deep copy operations

title: Keep related concurrent tasks in one lifecycle
summary: Concurrent child tasks need a bounded lifetime and a defined policy for cancellation and sibling failure.
guidance: Use structured task groups where appropriate so completion, exceptions, and cancellation cannot silently escape the owning scope.

title: Rubric: reason across state transitions
summary: A strong answer tracks which invariants hold before, during, and after mutation or an external call.
guidance: Score higher when the candidate identifies partial failure, retry, or repeated-call behavior instead of checking one isolated output.

citation.title: Clutch interview rubric: correctness state transitions

title: Question bank: run the operation twice
summary: Ask what changes when the function is called twice with the same input or partially updated state.
guidance: Look for shared state, idempotency, duplicate effects, and a test that distinguishes the first call from the second.

citation.title: Clutch question bank: repeat the operation

title: Use subtests for related input variations
summary: Related cases can share setup while still reporting which specific input failed.
guidance: Use a compact case table when behavior is the same across variations; keep distinct workflows in separate tests with descriptive names.

citation.title: Python unittest — Distinguishing test iterations using subtests

title: Test the exception contract explicitly
summary: Failure tests should verify the expected exception type and, when contractual, the useful diagnostic detail.
guidance: Trigger the smallest failure condition and avoid assertions so broad that an unrelated error satisfies the test.

title: Isolate the event loop used by async tests
summary: Async tests need lifecycle control so pending tasks and asynchronous cleanup do not leak between cases.
guidance: Use an async-aware test case or fixture, await the behavior under test, and clean up resources and background tasks deterministically.

title: Rubric: make a failing test diagnostic
summary: A good test failure identifies which contract broke without requiring the reader to replay the entire implementation.
guidance: Score higher when assertions are specific, cases have meaningful names, and failure output separates setup problems from behavior defects.

title: Question bank: investigate a flaky test
summary: Ask which uncontrolled dependency could make this test pass locally and fail intermittently in CI.
guidance: Look for time, randomness, ordering, shared state, concurrency, or network boundaries and a way to control the chosen source.

citation.title: Clutch question bank: flaky test investigation

title: Use data classes for explicit data-focused records
summary: Data classes can make a record's fields, defaults, equality, and representation explicit without hiding a larger behavior object.
guidance: Use them when the abstraction is primarily data, validate important invariants at construction, and avoid treating mutable records as universal domain models.

title: Represent closed choices explicitly
summary: An enumeration communicates that a value belongs to a finite named set instead of being an unconstrained string or number.
guidance: Use an enum when the set is genuinely closed and shared; preserve forward compatibility when external systems may add unknown values.

title: Use abstract contracts for shared behavior
summary: An abstract base class can state required behavior where nominal membership and shared implementation are part of the design.
guidance: Keep the contract narrow, prefer structural protocols when inheritance is unnecessary, and avoid a hierarchy without multiple real implementations.

title: Rubric: identify why responsibilities belong together
summary: A cohesive unit groups behavior that changes for the same reason and keeps unrelated policy or infrastructure at a boundary.
guidance: Score higher when the candidate names the shared responsibility and the concrete pressure for splitting or retaining the unit.

title: Question bank: replace one dependency
summary: Ask what must change if a database, clock, queue, or third-party client is replaced.
guidance: Look for the current coupling, the smallest stable contract, construction ownership, and tests that work through the boundary.

citation.title: Clutch question bank: replace a dependency

title: Use cryptographically secure randomness for secrets
summary: Tokens, reset links, and authentication secrets require randomness designed to resist prediction.
guidance: Use the secrets module or an equivalent cryptographic source, choose enough entropy, and do not substitute general simulation randomness.

citation.title: Python secrets — Generate secure random numbers

title: Compare authentication values without content-based timing
summary: Ordinary equality checks may reveal information about secret values through timing differences.
guidance: Use a constant-time comparison primitive for digests and authentication tokens, after normalizing types and lengths as the protocol requires.

title: Never deserialize untrusted pickle data
summary: Pickle data can execute arbitrary code during deserialization and is not a safe interchange format for untrusted input.
guidance: Choose a non-executable format with explicit schema validation, or authenticate trusted serialized data before loading it.

title: Rubric: bound the privilege of a failure
summary: A strong answer explains which capability the component needs and how damage is limited if its input or credential is compromised.
guidance: Score higher when permissions, secret scope, network reachability, and audit evidence are tied to the actual operation.

title: Question bank: trace a secret's lifecycle
summary: Ask where a credential is created, transported, used, logged, rotated, and revoked.
guidance: Look for minimum scope, redaction, storage boundaries, rotation behavior, and a response when the secret is exposed.
